summary: In Texas, new construction (new structures, added square footage, initial finish-out) and any work on residential property is not taxed to the customer under a lump-sum contract, while remodeling of existing nonresidential property is taxable on the total charge.

Remodeling, restoring or modifying residential real property (homes, apartments, nursing and retirement homes; not hotels), under a lump-sum contract
Remodeling, restoring or modifying existing nonresidential real property (offices, shops, restaurants, factories)

citations.title: Pub. 94-116, Real Property Repair and Remodeling (03/2007)
citations.quote: On the other hand, the total amount charged for remodeling, repairing, or restoring nonresidential real property is taxable.

citations.title: Pub. 94-116, Real Property Repair and Remodeling (03/2007)
citations.quote: Labor to repair, remodel, or restore residential real property is not taxable.

citations.title: Tex. Tax Code §151.056(a)
citations.quote: A contractor is the consumer of tangible personal property furnished by him and incorporated into the property of his customer if the contract between the contractor and his customer contains a lump-sum price covering both the performance of the service and the furnishing of the necessary incidental material.

citations.title: Tex. Tax Code §151.0047(a)
citations.quote: "Real property repair and remodeling" means the repair, restoration, remodeling, or modification of an improvement to real property other than: (1) a structure or separate part of a structure used as a residence;

notes: Under a lump-sum contract the contractor pays tax on materials and charges the customer none; under a separated contract the contractor collects tax on the separately stated materials (§151.056(b)), and the labor stays untaxed. A single-charge nonresidential job that adds square footage and remodels existing space is presumed taxable if the remodel is over 5% of the charge (Pub. 94-116). Texas city, county, transit and special-purpose district sales taxes apply to the same taxable items as the state tax (Tax Code ch. 321-323), so this rule covers the state and local parts alike.

notes: §151.0101(a)(5)(D) excludes from taxable services the creation, development and modification of a computer program 'not sold by the person performing' the work; a program the developer sells or licenses is a computer program, i.e. tangible personal property (§151.009).
